title: {{NAME}} and the Last Dragons of Dawn Valley
moral: Old magic and old giants still have much to teach us, if we know how to listen.

pages.content:
Dawn Valley was supposed to be extinct.

That is: the survey maps said nothing lived there. The geographers said the valley had been empty for thousands of years. The park rangers said the gates were locked and nobody went in.

The gates were locked. That part was true.

But on {{NAME}}'s map, drawn by his grandmother who had been a field naturalist for fifty years, there was a small note beside Dawn Valley in faded pencil: still there, if you know when to look.

He went at sunrise.

pages.content:
Two things lived in Dawn Valley.

First: a herd of young Brachiosaurus, their necks moving through the early mist like slow-motion fountains, feeding on the tops of enormous tree ferns.

Second, and considerably more surprising: a unicorn the colour of bone-white stone, old and quiet, with a horn that had gone silver-grey with age.

The unicorn stood at the centre of the herd. The Brachiosaurus moved around her without touching her, leaving a circle of quiet space.

She was, {{NAME}} realised, their keeper.

pages.content:
The unicorn's name, she showed him in a vision when he touched her horn, was a name that meant first morning.

She had been here since the valley was young. She had watched the dinosaurs and kept them safe. Her horn had no healing glow left in it, but it had something better: the sound it made when she walked kept the herd calm, kept predators at bay, kept the valley in its particular dreaming peace.

"You're their guardian," {{NAME}} said.

She touched his forehead with her horn, very gently.

He saw the valley as she saw it: a treasure that needed protecting.

pages.content:
He spent the day in the valley, drawing everything in his notebook: the herd's routes, the food sources, the old unicorn's movements.

The Brachiosaurus grew used to him by noon and one young one, smaller than the rest, followed him around for two hours, nudging his notebook with its snout.

"I'll keep your secret," {{NAME}} told the unicorn as the sun began to lower. "I promise."

She lowered her head once: a bow.

pages.content:
He found the gate again just as the light turned amber.

At home that night, he wrote three pages of notes, then closed his notebook and put it away.

Some records were not for sharing.

He lay in the dark, thinking of the valley under its blanket of stars, the Brachiosaurus folded up in the mist, the old unicorn moving quietly between them.

A first morning. Still going.

He closed his eyes, and slept better than he had in months.
